description.summary: Azure AI Search is a fully managed cloud search service with exact and HNSW vector retrieval, OData filtering, BM25-vector hybrid search, reciprocal-rank fusion, semantic reranking, and integrated indexing and vectorization pipelines.
description.description: Azure AI Search is a Microsoft Azure platform service for indexing and querying search documents through lexical, vector, hybrid, semantic, filtered, and agent-oriented retrieval APIs. Vector fields support exhaustive K-nearest-neighbor search and HNSW approximate nearest-neighbor search with cosine, dot-product, or Euclidean similarity. Built-in scalar and binary quantization can reduce memory and storage, with optional oversampling and rescoring against preserved full-precision vectors. Hybrid requests execute keyword and one or more vector queries in parallel and merge their ranked lists through reciprocal rank fusion; semantic ranker can then rerank text-rich candidates. OData filters target filterable nonvector fields and can be applied before or after vector traversal, with distinct recall and latency implications. Indexer and skillset pipelines can extract, chunk, enrich, and vectorize supported data sources by calling external embedding models, while query-time vectorizers can transform text or images into vectors. Capacity is provisioned through partitions and replicas, with managed replication, availability-zone placement where supported, Microsoft Entra ID, role-based access control, private endpoints, and encryption options. Azure AI Search is not intended to replace a primary system of record: indexing and replica propagation are asynchronous, document actions are reported independently, and the service does not provide native self-service backup and restore.

indexingConsiderations: Choose HNSW or exhaustive KNN only after measuring recall, latency, vector-index quota, indexing throughput, and cost on representative data.
Align cosine, dot-product, or Euclidean similarity with the embedding model and normalize vectors where the selected metric requires it.
Evaluate scalar or binary quantization, truncation dimensions, preserved originals, oversampling, and rescoring together rather than as isolated switches.
Model vector fields, searchable text, filterable metadata, semantic configurations, scoring profiles, analyzers, and security fields as one versioned index schema.
Distinguish preFilter, postFilter, and preview strictPostFilter because shard-level execution changes recall, latency, and top-k completeness.
Use exhaustive queries on sampled data to build ground truth for HNSW recall evaluation.
Tune HNSW construction and query parameters, vector weights, candidate k, text recall size, semantic reranking, and result thresholds under representative load.
Provision partitions for storage and indexing scale and replicas for query throughput and availability; test the combined search-unit configuration.
Treat integrated vectorization as a distributed pipeline that depends on data sources, indexers, skillsets, chunking logic, external embedding endpoints, identities, quotas, and retry behavior.
Version the data-plane API, management API, SDKs, index schema, vector profiles, compression settings, embedding models, and semantic configuration together.
Design index aliases or blue-green index deployment for structural schema changes that require rebuilds.
Keep an authoritative external data source and a tested reindex path because Azure AI Search is not a primary data store and has no native self-service backup and restore.
Use Microsoft Entra ID, least-privilege roles, private endpoints, managed identities, and customer-managed keys according to the workload threat model.
Measure indexing-to-query freshness and replica convergence separately from successful document-write acknowledgements.

limitations: Azure AI Search is a managed Azure service; availability, quotas, features, API versions, and costs vary by region, pricing tier, service creation date, and preview status.
HNSW consumes vector-index quota and trades recall, latency, indexing time, and memory; exhaustive KNN provides exact retrieval but can be computationally expensive.
Scalar and binary quantization are lossy unless mitigated through oversampling and rescoring, and truncation is appropriate only for compatible embedding models.
Post-filter and strict-post-filter modes can return false negatives or fewer than k results for selective filters, especially across multiple shards.
Semantic ranker reranks an existing candidate set rather than searching the full corpus and adds regional, quota, latency, and billing considerations.
Integrated vectorization depends on external embedding models and supported indexer data sources; Azure AI Search does not host the embedding models itself.
Replica propagation and index updates are asynchronous, so queries can temporarily observe incomplete results and unreplicated writes can be at risk during a primary-zone failure.
The service exposes per-document indexing results rather than general multi-document or multi-index ACID transaction semantics.

Azure AI Search is not designed as a primary system of record and does not provide native self-service backup and restore; recovery normally rebuilds indexes from authoritative source data or custom exports.
Partitions and replicas improve capacity and resilience but increase cost, and SLA eligibility requires minimum replica counts.
usageGuidance: Use Azure AI Search when a managed Azure-native service should combine lexical, vector, filtered, semantic, and agent-oriented retrieval behind one operational endpoint.
Prefer a dedicated vector database or self-hosted engine when portability, low-level index control, local execution, or non-Azure deployment is a primary requirement.
Benchmark pure lexical, pure vector, hybrid RRF, vector weighting, semantic reranking, compression, and filtering on the same relevance judgments.
Test ingestion, indexer retries, embedding throttling, query load, replica failover, zone behavior, index rebuild, alias cutover, and recovery before production adoption.
Record stable and preview API dependencies explicitly and avoid treating preview-only capabilities as generally available.

claims.statement: Azure AI Search supports vector fields with exhaustive K-nearest-neighbor retrieval and HNSW approximate nearest-neighbor search using cosine, dot-product, or Euclidean similarity, plus scalar or binary quantization with optional oversampling, rescoring, and dimension truncation.

qualifiers.name: versionScope
qualifiers.value: Azure AI Search stable data-plane API 2026-04-01 and official documentation accessed 2026-07-17

claims.rationale: Official vector-search, ranking, compression, API-version, and release documentation describes the currently stable vector schema and query capabilities.

claims.statement: Azure AI Search applies OData filters over filterable nonvector fields and supports vector pre-filtering and post-filtering, while strict post-filtering remains preview and has the highest false-negative risk for selective filters or small k values.

qualifiers.name: filterScope
qualifiers.value: Filter behavior depends on index creation date, vectorFilterMode, field attributes, shard count, selectivity, k, and stable versus preview API support

claims.rationale: The official filtering documentation distinguishes preFilter, postFilter, and preview strictPostFilter execution and explains their shard-level recall and latency tradeoffs.

claims.statement: Azure AI Search executes lexical and vector queries in parallel for hybrid search, merges ranked lists through Reciprocal Rank Fusion, supports vector weighting and multiple vector queries, and can apply semantic ranking to rerank text-rich hybrid or vector candidates.

qualifiers.name: rankingScope
qualifiers.value: Candidate counts, vector weights, text recall size, semantic configuration, regional availability, quotas, and billing require workload-specific evaluation

claims.rationale: Hybrid-scoring and semantic-ranking documentation describes RRF, vector weighting, multiple query lists, separate reranker scores, and semantic reranking after initial retrieval.

claims.statement: Azure AI Search can create indexing pipelines that extract, chunk, enrich, and vectorize supported source content by using indexers and skillsets, while query-time vectorizers call external embedding models; the search service itself does not host embedding models.

qualifiers.name: pipelineScope
qualifiers.value: Integrated vectorization depends on supported data sources, indexers, skillsets, external model endpoints, managed identities, model quotas, and API-version compatibility

claims.rationale: Integrated-vectorization and embedding documentation separates search-managed orchestration from external model hosting and describes chunking, skillsets, vector fields, and query vectorizers.

claims.statement: Azure AI Search is a managed service that scales through partitions and replicas, uses asynchronous replica propagation, provides document-level indexing results and Azure security controls, and is designed to be rebuilt from an authoritative data source rather than used as a primary database with native self-service backup and restore.

qualifiers.name: operationsScope
qualifiers.value: Effective availability, durability, security, recovery, and cost depend on pricing tier, replica and partition counts, region, zone support, client retries, external source data, and tested rebuild procedures

claims.rationale: Capacity, reliability, index, document API, authentication, networking, and encryption documentation describes service units, replication, SLA thresholds, per-document results, primary-store boundaries, recovery patterns, and security controls.

evidence.summary: Microsoft documentation describes exact exhaustive KNN and HNSW ANN vector retrieval, three similarity metrics, scalar and binary quantization, oversampling, rescoring, and optional dimension truncation.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can represent Azure AI Search as a managed vector search service with both exact and graph-based retrieval plus built-in compression controls.

sourceFragments.locator: Exhaustive KNN and HNSW algorithms, metrics, memory, recall, and query behavior
Scalar and binary quantization, oversampling, rescoring, and truncation dimensions

limitations: Official product documentation is not an independent recall, latency, cost, or scalability benchmark.
Compression, metric, dimensions, HNSW settings, vector quota, oversampling, and preserved-original configuration materially affect quality and cost.

evidence.summary: Azure AI Search documents preFilter as the recommended default for newer indexes, postFilter as shard-local candidate filtering, and strictPostFilter as a preview mode that filters the unfiltered global top k.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark metadata filtering as supported while warning that execution placement changes recall, latency, and result completeness.

sourceFragments.locator: preFilter, postFilter, and preview strictPostFilter semantics and tradeoffs
Vector search combined with filters over nonvector fields

limitations: Vector fields themselves are not filterable; filters target filterable nonvector fields in the same index.
Selective filters, small k values, and multiple shards can produce false negatives or fewer results in post-filter modes.

evidence.summary: Azure AI Search hybrid-search documentation describes parallel lexical and vector retrieval, RRF list merging, vector weighting, multiple vector queries, and semantic reranking with a separate reranker score.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can represent BM25-plus-vector hybrid retrieval, RRF, multi-vector retrieval, and semantic reranking as first-class managed capabilities.

sourceFragments.locator: RRF merging, vector weighting, subscores, candidate counts, and semantic reranking after fusion
Semantic ranker reranks an existing top candidate set and returns captions or answers from indexed text
Hybrid keyword and vector queries execute in parallel

limitations: Semantic ranker does not rerun retrieval over the entire corpus and generally reranks only the existing top candidate set.
RRF, vector weights, candidate k, lexical recall size, semantic configuration, quotas, latency, and billing require workload-specific evaluation.

evidence.summary: Microsoft documentation describes indexer and skillset pipelines for extraction, chunking, enrichment, and vectorization plus query-time vectorizers that call external embedding models.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can distinguish managed ingestion orchestration from model hosting and record integrated vectorization as an indexing and query integration rather than an embedded model runtime.

evidence.summary: Azure AI Search documentation describes partition-and-replica capacity, asynchronous replica propagation, SLA replica thresholds, per-document write statuses, primary-store boundaries, rebuild-based recovery, RBAC, private endpoints, and customer-managed encryption keys.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark high managed scalability and security while recording eventual consistency, document-level write semantics, and variable backup and restore capabilities.

limitations: Azure AI Search is a secondary search index, so authoritative source retention and a tested rebuild or export process remain the customer's responsibility.
Asynchronous replication can expose temporary staleness, and writes not yet replicated from a failed primary can be lost during a zone failure.
